One idea carries the whole piece: early computing seen as a signal that is breaking down and burning, shown through glitch scanlines, a macro shot of a chip grid and a glowing red disc that reads as a hot die or a lens
The palette commits fully to saturated red and magenta, and it is clearly motivated by heat and danger rather than used as decoration
The texture is real and analogue: CRT smear, dust and burn on the disc, a fine grid of circuitry, with depth and material in every frame
The type has a point of view: a small classic serif for 'AMC presents' contrasts with a heavy, tracked, extended title next to a square cursor glyph that reads as a terminal prompt
The frames progress from noise to structure to a single resolved object, which implies choreography and an arc
gaps: The serif credit sits loosely over the glitch field; it could be tied into the image more tightly
The middle frame's four-square symbol is a bit literal (a chip or a logo) next to the more poetic opening and closing frames
Range is narrow: almost every frame is the same red register, which risks monotony over the full length

The busiest frame reaches visual overload: legibility and hierarchy collapse instead of resolving into a poster-grade final frame

Typography is chosen for period and meaning: a refined serif for 'AMC presents' against an extended, tracked grotesk title with a small block-cursor glyph
The frames move from chaos (glitch) to order (chip quadrants) to a single focal burn, which shows deliberate choreography with weight
gaps: The middle frame's four-square chip is close to a literal diagram; one more layer of material detail would lift it to the level of the other frames

The vocabulary stays within a single gesture (glitch to burn); a second surprising beat would make it more memorable

tells: Mixes media across frames: a live-action station platform with a motion-blurred train and a composited bespoke 'D' poster, then a liquid-chrome fluid simulation, then a flat red type card. That range points to a studio collaboration, not a template.
The fluid-sim frame has real material complexity: iridescent oil-slick refraction, ejecta droplets and thin ligaments. It is credited to a named artist (Thomas Traum).
The red/black/white palette carries from the poster in frame 1 to the 'Eike König' wordmark, so the identity holds across very different worlds.
The poster sits convincingly in the real scene, with matched perspective and light.
Weakness: the end card is a plain centred bold-grotesk name on grey. It is deliberate brand restraint, but it is the least designed frame.
gaps: The three frames read as separate showcase vignettes. Unlike C, there is no single idea or recurring device carrying through the piece.
The final type card is a standard centred lockup. Let the letterform take part in the motion (e.g. the 'D' from frame 1 resolving into the name) rather than just appearing.
The palette jumps from cool daylight to pale-blue CG to neutral grey. C commits to one hue and gets far more atmosphere from it.

tells: Custom modular display type that breaks Latin and katakana into the same geometric strokes. It is a real typographic idea (bilingual Tokyo signage turned into a glyph system), not default fonts.
Dense, layered frames: grids, dot matrices, scan-bars, registration marks and offset colour plates. Each frame is built differently.
Unusual palette of hot pink, acid lime, slate and violet with grain and print-like misregistration.
Clear progression between frames, from a single glyph in close-up to a scrambled text field to a resolved 'TOKYO' composite, which shows deliberate choreography of decoding.
gaps: The light is all graphic and flat. Unlike C's glowing, burnt red, there is no sense of a physical light source or optical depth.
The glitch/cyber-signage language is a well-worn genre. One unexpected image or material would make it stand apart.
The resolved title frame is busy enough to lose hierarchy. Give the payoff the same clear figure/ground C gives 'HALT AND CATCH FIRE'.

tells: A specific conceptual idea: early-computing hardware (circuit grid, chip-like blocks, CRT/oscilloscope glow) rendered as one burning red signal. The title 'Halt and Catch Fire' is a machine instruction, and the image literally overheats.
A near-monochrome red with a full tonal range, from hot pink-white to deep oxblood. It is a committed, memorable palette choice.
Real texture and light: scan-line tearing, phosphor bloom, a vignetted circular lens/sun with organic mottling. It looks optical and analogue, not vector.
Restrained, well-placed typography: a small serif 'AMC presents' tucked into the glitch, and a tracked wide-sans title with a cursor block, set small against a huge glowing field.
The frames progress from chaos to grid to a single glowing disc, which implies a strong arc of resolution.
gaps: The middle frame's four-square grid is the plainest image in the piece. It could carry more of the burnt, analogue texture.
Type is mostly left to support the image. A more ownable title treatment would bring typography up to the level of the image.
Variety of motion between frames is implied rather than shown. Clearer changes of scale or camera would strengthen the sense of choreography.

defects: Final lockup holds about 4.8 s with almost no change (per-second change drops to 12 → 7 → 4). That is dead air, not a deliberate settle.
Faint ghost columns of leftover squares stay under the pixel wordmark at 100%, like an unfinished fade-out or stray low-opacity layer.
The note grid moves sideways at a constant rate, with no easing and no motion blur between the paired frames. The blocks slide like a sequencer playhead instead of having weight.
Freeze-frames fail as posters: the '01' frame is mostly empty, and 'AY' is cropped mid-wipe.
There are too many type voices: pixel display, grotesk, mono staff labels, an ultra-wide black display face with outline echoes, and rotated vertical text.
Pairs on the final lockup show the dither squares and the artist list barely changing, so the last third adds no new information.
Audio looks thin: one-shot plucks with few partials, a fixed click grid and short noise bursts, with little low-mid body and no clear mix arc.
Energy peaks around 55% (cuts at about 4 s and 6 s), then drops off sharply instead of building to a peak and releasing.
gaps: Choreography: the staff-to-wordmark idea is good but never shown on screen. Notes should visibly fly in and lock into the OCTAVA pixel letters in one continuous move, with eased weight and overshoot, instead of cutting from grid to type.
Timing: cut the 4.8 s end hold to about 1.5 s with a final accent hit. Move the densest beat (the 2027/BASEL echo stack) to 65–75% so the piece actually builds and releases.

Sound and finish: replace the sparse synth plucks with a produced arrangement, including real instrument timbre, a low end and a riser into the lockup. Add material (paper grain, light falloff on the blocks) and remove the ghost-square artefacts so the frames hold up at 100%.
